name: Iris Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Iris. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Copperleaf Design, four of us above the stationer's on Church Lane. Most of what I do is wedding stationery, the parish and school newsletters, and logos for family businesses like the butcher and the funeral directors on the high street. I always start with a pencil, because I do a lot of hand lettering, and then I scan it in and tidy it on the computer. What wears me out is couples changing the date font for the fifth time three weeks before the wedding.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No, never. Graham, who owns Copperleaf, tried one once and it put six fingers on a bride, and we both had a good laugh. I'd rather work for less with my own hands than be paid to press a button. Maybe that makes me old-fashioned at twenty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because it was always oversold. At church and with friends I'd say real craft is still worth paying for. I don't post online much, but if I did it'd be pictures of my lettering, not opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means nothing changes for me, and that suits me. People don't hire Copperleaf Design for wedding invitations because it's quick. They hire us because my boss Graham will sit with them over tea for an hour. I've got about three months saved and steady work, so I'm comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing exactly what I do. Daniel and I would keep saving for the house deposit and for the wedding next September. I might take a weekend calligraphy class to get better at the gold-ink work brides ask for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Relieved, I think, that the people who said it would change everything were wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything in your work a worry, even in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Graham's sixty-three, so one day he'll want to retire, and I don't know who'd take on Copperleaf. That's in the back of my mind. But it's years away, and it's got nothing to do with computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to happen when Graham retires?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to buy Copperleaf off Graham one day, if I'm honest. Daniel's dad ran his own electrical firm, and I like the idea of a family business. We'd need a lot more saved first.

say: AI was always **oversold**, so it's good it stalled.
**Real craft** is still worth paying for, which I'd say at church and with friends.
think: Nothing changes for me, and that **suits me** fine.
Clients come to Copperleaf for **Graham's time** and care, not for speed.
do: Keep saving with Daniel for the **house deposit** and next September's wedding.
Take a weekend **calligraphy class** to improve gold-ink lettering for brides.
feel: **Calm** and a bit **relieved** that the big promises were wrong.
S0.quote: People don't hire Copperleaf Design for wedding invitations because it's quick. They hire us because my boss Graham will sit with them over tea for an hour.
fieldNote: Her security rests on **personal service**: clients pay for time and conversation, not speed.
The only cloud is Graham's **retirement**, which she'd like to answer by buying the business.
A traditional, **family-business** instinct shapes how she pictures her future.

steps.text: Keep hand-lettering wedding stationery at Copperleaf
Save with Daniel for the house deposit and wedding
Take a weekend calligraphy class in gold-ink lettering

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people will learn the hard way that cheap isn't the same as good. At church I'd probably say it's a shame, that families used to come to a person. I wouldn't say anything online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it hurts us badly. If a bride can get wedding invitations from an app for twenty pounds, the bride will, and my boss Graham can't price a pot of tea against that. The newsletters would go too, because the school secretary would just type it into something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back straight away, no more takeaways, no new clothes for the hen weekend. I'd ask Graham to let me lean harder on the hand-made side, letterpress and calligraphy, because that's the only bit a machine can't fake well. I wouldn't learn the AI tools. I'd look into evening work doing painted signs for pubs, which Daniel's uncle says there's still call for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like the ground's a bit softer than I thought.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't learning the tools keep you in work longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, and I know that sounds stubborn. Graham's agreed with me on it, and the people who come to us come because we don't. The day we're just another app, there's no reason to come up Church Lane at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big companies that build these things and sell them to everyone for pennies. And honestly people who want something for nothing. But I'd not want the government stepping in with handouts either; I'd want people to choose to pay for good work.

say: People will learn **cheap isn't the same** as good.
It's a **shame** families stop coming to a real person, which I'd say at church.
think: **Wedding clients** would pick a twenty-pound app over Copperleaf's prices.
The **school and parish newsletters** would go too, typed straight into software.
do: Cut **takeaways and new clothes**, including for the hen weekend.
Ask Graham to push the **hand-made side**, letterpress and calligraphy.
Look into **painted pub signs** in the evenings, through Daniel's uncle.
feel: **Anxious**, like the ground is softer than she thought.
S1.quote: If a bride can get wedding invitations from an app for twenty pounds, the bride will, and my boss Graham can't price a pot of tea against that.
fieldNote: She refuses the tools on **principle** and sees that as the agency's whole selling point.
She blames **big tech** and bargain hunters but rejects **handouts** as the answer.
Her backup is **craft and hands-on** work rather than learning AI.

steps.text: Stop takeaways and skip new clothes for the hen weekend
Push letterpress and calligraphy work at Copperleaf
Paint pub signs in the evenings through Daniel's uncle

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should pray about it and look after each other, because nobody's ready. At work I'd tell Graham we need to talk about how long Copperleaf can last. I'd stay off the internet; it'd be all shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'm out of a job in a year, maybe sooner. Wedding stationery and newsletters are exactly the sort of desk work it'd take first. The hand lettering might hang on as a hobby people pay a little for, but not a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the wedding spending now. I'd marry my fiancé Daniel at the town hall instead of the church hall do, and we'd keep the house deposit in the bank. I'd ask Daniel to help me get on an electrical apprenticeship, or anything with my hands, because the robots don't come till about 2031 in this one. And I'd keep three months of savings untouched for as long as I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. It feels like the floor going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel's work is hands-on, so he'd have a few years more than me. My parents would help where they could, and the church would rally round. I'd want family and community before any government scheme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like I said, the town hall. My mother would be upset, she's been planning the church hall reception for two years. But I'd rather start married life with money in the bank than a nice day and no job.

say: We should **pray** and look after each other, because **nobody's ready**.
I'd tell Graham we need to talk about **how long Copperleaf** can last.
think: I'm **out of a job** within about a year.
Hand lettering might survive as a **paid hobby**, but not a wage.
do: Cut **wedding spending** and marry at the town hall instead.
Ask Daniel to help find an **electrical apprenticeship** before robots come in 2031.
Keep **three months of savings** untouched as long as possible.
S2.quote: I'd marry my fiancé Daniel at the town hall instead of the church hall do, and we'd keep the house deposit in the bank.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job** within a year and turns to a hands-on trade.
She'd lean on **family and church** first, before any government scheme.
Downsizing the wedding is a real **sacrifice**; her mother has planned it for two years.

steps.text: Hold the wedding at the town hall, not the church hall
Apply for an electrical apprenticeship with Daniel's help
Ask parents and church friends for help through the change
Keep three months of savings untouched

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been warned, so there's no excuse not to get ready. To friends I'd say learn a trade, like our grandparents did. I'd still not go on about it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's the same as the fast one, just later. My fiancé Daniel has always said I'd make a good electrician, and I always laughed. In five years I might not be laughing. It's not what I trained for, but it's honest work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Copperleaf for now, because Graham needs me and the work's still there for a couple of years. In year two I'd start an evening course in electrical installation at the college. We'd still have the church wedding but cheaper, and we'd buy a smaller house so the mortgage works on one wage if it has to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steadier. Five years is enough to learn a trade if I don't dawdle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the AI tools to stay in design longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. If I'm leaving design anyway, I'd rather learn something that'll last a few more years than something that'll be gone by 2031. I'd let the young ones do the AI bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you tell Graham?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Graham early, so he could plan. He'd understand, he's always said a trade is a good thing to have. I think he'd probably retire when I go.

say: We've **been warned**, so there's no excuse not to get ready.
Learn **a trade** like our grandparents did, which I'd tell friends.
think: The design job still ends, just **later**.
**Electrical work** isn't what I trained for, but it's honest work.
do: Keep working at Copperleaf for **a couple of years** while the work lasts.
Start an evening **electrical installation** course in year two.
Buy a **smaller house** so the mortgage works on **one wage**.
feel: **Anxious** but steadier, because five years is enough to learn a trade.
S3.quote: My fiancé Daniel has always said I'd make a good electrician, and I always laughed. In five years I might not be laughing.
fieldNote: Five years lets her **plan a trade** rather than scramble, and she'd still marry in church.
She still won't learn AI, preferring skills that **last longer**.
She'd tell her boss **early**, out of loyalty to him.

steps.text: Keep working at Copperleaf for the next two years
Start an evening electrical installation course in year two
Buy a smaller house the mortgage can carry on one wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and plenty can change, so let's not lose our heads. At work I'd say keep doing good work. I'd not say anything online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, by 2036 I'd hope to have a child or two and be home with them for a few years, the way my mum was. Daniel's trade would carry us until about 2039. So the design job ending then might matter less to me than to someone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Copperleaf and keep saving hard with Daniel, for the house and for when the children come. I'd not rush into anything. I'd maybe do the calligraphy class and keep the hand lettering going as a little sideline for later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not frightened. It feels far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And when robots come for Daniel's work in 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the worry, yes. We'd need savings by then. I don't want my children growing up thinking a screen made everything. I want them to see someone's hands do the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do anything differently now, with ten years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to see what's actually happening first. Ten years ago people said lots of things would happen that didn't. If by year five it looks real, I'd start the electrical course then.

say: Ten years is **a long time**, so let's not lose our heads.
I'd tell people at work to **keep doing good work**.
think: By 2036 I hope to be **home with children**, like my mum was.
**Daniel's trade** would carry us until about 2039.
do: Carry on at Copperleaf and **save hard** with Daniel for the house and children.
Keep **hand lettering** going as a small sideline for later.
Wait until **year five** before starting the electrical course.
feel: **Uneasy** but not frightened, because it feels far away.
S4.quote: I don't want my children growing up thinking a screen made everything. I want them to see someone's hands do the work.
fieldNote: Her family plans make the 2036 date **matter less**; she expects to be home with children.
Resistant to change, she'd **wait and see** until year five before retraining.
She still worries about **2039**, when Daniel's hands-on trade is reached.

steps.text: Carry on lettering wedding stationery at Copperleaf
Save hard with Daniel for the house and children
Decide on the electrical course only in year five

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no question, because it would come before the wedding and before I could learn anything else. What would help is apprenticeships for people my age, paid ones, so you can earn while you learn a trade. And I'd want families and churches to be at the centre of it, not just a government cheque.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether I'd ever give in and use the tools. I don't think so. I'd rather work for less with my own hands than be paid to press a button. Maybe that makes me old-fashioned at twenty-seven.

headlineQuote: I'd rather work for less with my own hands than be paid to press a button. Maybe that makes me old-fashioned at twenty-seven.
portrait: Iris is a 27-year-old designer at **Copperleaf Design**, doing wedding stationery, newsletters and logos for family firms.
She **never uses AI**, works from pencil sketches and hand lettering, and sees craft as her value.
She's engaged to **Daniel**, an electrician, and they're saving for a wedding and a house deposit.
As AGI gets closer she turns to an **electrical trade**, leaning on family and church rather than government.
She's **calm** if AI stalls, **alarmed** in the fast version, and less worried with a decade's warning.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it would land before the wedding and before she could learn a trade.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** for people her age to earn while learning a trade.
**Families and churches** at the centre of the response, not just a government cheque.
